content: Hospitalized patients are at an elevated risk of developing deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in the veins of the lower limbs and pelvis. This increased risk is primarily due to prolonged immobility associated with their medical or surgical conditions. Patients who develop DVT are at a higher risk of experiencing a pulmonary embolism (PE), a potentially life-threatening complication. Graduated compression stockings (GCS) have been proposed as a preventive measure to reduce the risk of DVT in hospitalized patients. This review aimed to evaluate the effectiveness and safety of GCS in preventing DVT across various groups of hospitalized patients. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of GCS alone or in combination with other DVT prophylactic methods. Data from these trials were analyzed using rigorous statistical methods, and the quality of evidence was assessed using the GRADE system. A total of 20 RCTs were included in the review, involving 1681 participants and 1172 individual legs, resulting in 2853 analytic units. Among these trials, 10 focused on patients undergoing general surgery, six on orthopedic surgery, and one each on neurosurgery, cardiac surgery, gynecological surgery, and medical patients. GCS were typically applied either the day before surgery or on the day of surgery and were worn until discharge or until the patient regained full mobility. The duration of follow-up ranged from seven to 14 days. Most studies used the radioactive I125 uptake test to identify DVT, and the overall risk of bias in the included studies was low. The pooled data from 20 studies showed that 9% of units in the GCS group developed DVT (134 of 1445 units), compared to 21% in the control group without GCS (290 of 1408 units). The Peto odds ratio (OR) was 0.35 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.28 to 0.43), indicating a significant reduction in DVT risk with GCS use (P < 0.001). This evidence was of high quality. For proximal DVT, data from eight studies showed that 1% of units in the GCS group (7 of 517) developed proximal DVT, compared to 5% in the control group (28 of 518). The Peto OR was 0.26 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.53), again favoring GCS use (P < 0.001). However, the quality of evidence for proximal DVT was downgraded to moderate due to the low event rate and imprecision. Regarding pulmonary embolism (PE), data from five studies involving surgical patients showed that 2% of participants in the GCS group (5 of 283) developed PE, compared to 5% in the control group (14 of 286). The Peto OR was 0.38 (95% CI 0.15 to 0.96), favoring GCS use (P = 0.04). However, the quality of evidence for PE was considered low due to the low event rate and lack of routine screening for PE. Subgroup analysis of surgical patients (19 trials) revealed that 9.8% of units in the GCS group (134 of 1365) developed DVT, compared to 21.2% in the control group (282 of 1328). The Peto OR was 0.35 (95% CI 0.28 to 0.44), with high-quality evidence supporting the use of GCS (P < 0.001). For proximal DVT in surgical patients, 1.6% of units in the GCS group (7 of 437) developed proximal DVT, compared to 6.4% in the control group (28 of 438). The Peto OR was 0.26 (95% CI 0.13 to 0.53), with moderate-quality evidence favoring GCS use (P < 0.001). In medical patients, data from one trial involving individuals admitted after acute myocardial infarction showed that no legs in the GCS group (0 of 80) developed DVT, compared to 10% in the control group (8 of 80). The Peto OR was 0.12 (95% CI 0.03 to 0.51), favoring GCS use (P = 0.004). However, no cases of proximal DVT or PE were reported in this trial, and the quality of evidence was low. Adverse effects and complications associated with GCS use were not routinely or quantitatively reported in the included studies, limiting the ability to assess their incidence accurately. In conclusion, there is high-quality evidence that GCS are effective in reducing the risk of DVT in hospitalized patients undergoing general or orthopedic surgery, with or without additional thromboprophylaxis. There is moderate-quality evidence suggesting that GCS likely reduce the risk of proximal DVT and low-quality evidence indicating that GCS may reduce the risk of PE. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of GCS in preventing DVT in medical patients.
